title: The hot hand
lede: The hot hand is the belief that a basketball shooter who has just made several shots is more likely to make the next. A 1985 study called it a fallacy; a 2018 reanalysis showed that study's test was biased, and that corrected, its own data show a hot hand.

sections.heading: The 1985 verdict
sections.body: In 1985 the psychologists Thomas Gilovich, Robert Vallone and Amos Tversky tested the belief that a player is more likely to score after a make [1]. They surveyed 100 basketball fans at Cornell and Stanford, studied the field goals of the 1980-81 Philadelphia 76ers, analyzed free throws, and ran a controlled shooting experiment [1]. In every study the outcomes of shots were independent of each other [2]. Their reading: sequences of makes and misses look just like sequences of coin flips, and the hot hand is a cognitive illusion [3]. For about 30 years that was the consensus, and Daniel Kahneman called the hot hand "a massive and widespread cognitive illusion" [4].

sections.heading: The flaw in the test
sections.body: The 1985 test compared how often players hit after a streak of hits with how often they hit after a streak of misses, and assumed a coin-like shooter would show no gap [1]. In 2018 Joshua Miller and Adam Sanjurjo proved that this common measure is biased in finite sequences [2]. Toss a coin four times, score the share of heads that follow a heads, and average over the sequences that can be scored: the expected value is 40.5%, not 50% [3]. The bias shrinks as sequences get longer, grows with the length of the streak, and stays substantial at sequence lengths often used in empirical work [2]. The cause is selection: picking which flips to study by where the streaks are changes the odds [4].

sections.heading: What the data say now
sections.body: In the 1985 data, shooting after three or more makes was only three percentage points better than after three or more misses. Measured against what a coin would really produce, that gap is 11 percentage points higher, a substantial and statistically significant hot hand [1]. In Miller and Sanjurjo's words, "the longstanding conclusions of the canonical study are reversed" [2]. Other data point the same way: more than 300,000 NBA free throws from five seasons showed strong evidence at the individual level [3], and a 2021 study of NBA Three-Point Contests from 1986 to 2020 found considerable evidence of hot hand shooting [4].

sections.heading: How big it is
sections.body: A real hot hand is not necessarily a big one. The evidence suggests only a small subset of players shows it, and among those who do the effect size tends to be small [1]. It may hold only for runs of shots from one spot, such as free throws or the Three-Point Contest, and not for field goals in games [2]. A 2014 paper at the Sloan Sports Analytics Conference, which controlled for shot location and defender position, found a "small yet significant hot-hand effect" [3]. And a 2003 power analysis of the 1985 data concluded that even if the 76ers did shoot in streaks, the original tests would have been unlikely to find it [4].

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: The 1985 result shaped how psychologists and economists think about decisions where information arrives over time, and the hot hand fallacy was carried into financial investing and video gaming [1]. The bias Miller and Sanjurjo found is not about basketball: it sits in a common measure of how outcomes depend on streaks in any sequential data [2]. It also sharpens what the fallacy means. A hot hand and a hot hand fallacy can coexist: a player can shoot better after makes while people believe the boost is bigger than it is [3]. Gilovich, one of the 1985 authors, said the new paper had identified something new in a 30-year debate [4].

fights.note: The fallacy was about belief all along, and that evidence is untouched by the bias.
fights.body: The hot hand fallacy still stands. Gilovich, an author of the 1985 study, accepts that streak data are biased in small samples but says "I don't think it's a very big effect" in the NBA data sets that have been studied [1]. And the fallacy was always about belief. In the 1985 betting study, 26 varsity players took 100 shots each and predicted every one [2]. Making the last shot correlated r = .40 with predicting a make, but only r = .05 with actually making it [3]. That comparison is not touched by the streak selection bias, and people still see far more streakiness than exists [4].
